question: Which of the following is an example of a combination reaction?
solution:
The correct answer is __**CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Combination Reaction** is a type of chemical reaction where **two or more reactants** (elements or compounds) combine to form a **single product**. The general representation is **A + B → AB**.
 
• **CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2**: In this reaction, **Calcium Oxide** (also known as **Quick Lime**) reacts vigorously with **Water** to produce **Calcium Hydroxide** (known as **Slaked Lime**). Since two reactants combine to form one single product, it is a classic example of a **Combination Reaction**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2**: This reaction involves **Zinc** displacing **Hydrogen** from **Sulphuric Acid**. This is an example of a **Single Displacement Reaction**, not a combination reaction. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **2KClO3 → 2KCl + 3O2**: In this case, a single reactant, **Potassium Chlorate**, breaks down into two simpler products, **Potassium Chloride** and **Oxygen**, usually upon heating. This is a **Decomposition Reaction**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **CuSO4 + BaCl2 → BaSO4 + CuCl2**: This reaction involves the exchange of ions between **Copper(II) Sulphate** and **Barium Chloride** to form **Barium Sulphate** and **Copper(II) Chloride**. It is categorized as a **Double Displacement Reaction** or a **Precipitation Reaction**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Exothermic Nature of Combination Reactions:** Many combination reactions, such as the reaction of **Quick Lime** with **Water**, release a significant amount of heat. Such reactions are called **Exothermic Reactions**. This specific reaction is used in **whitewashing** walls, where the **Slaked Lime** reacts slowly with **Carbon Dioxide** in the air to form a thin layer of **Calcium Carbonate**.
 
• **Decomposition Reactions:** These are the opposite of combination reactions. A single substance splits into two or more substances. This process usually requires energy in the form of **heat** (Thermal Decomposition), **light** (Photolysis), or **electricity** (Electrolysis). For example, the electrolysis of **Water (H2O)** yields **Hydrogen** and **Oxygen** gases.
 
• **Displacement Reactions:** A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. The **Reactivity Series** is used to determine which metal can displace another. For instance, **Iron (Fe)** can displace **Copper (Cu)** from a **Copper Sulphate (CuSO4)** solution because Iron is more reactive.
 
• **Double Displacement Reactions:** These occur when two ionic compounds in solution react by exchanging their **cations** and **anions**. Often, one of the products formed is an **insoluble solid** called a **precipitate**, as seen with **Barium Sulphate (BaSO4)** in the reaction between Barium Chloride and sodium sulphate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chemical Equations:** A chemical equation must always be **balanced** to satisfy the **Law of Conservation of Mass**, which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
 
• **Oxidation and Reduction (Redox):** Most chemical reactions also involve the transfer of electrons. **Oxidation** is the gain of **Oxygen** or loss of **Hydrogen/Electrons**, while **Reduction** is the loss of **Oxygen** or gain of **Hydrogen/Electrons**.
 
• **Physical States:** In chemical equations, symbols like **(s)** for solid, **(l)** for liquid, **(g)** for gas, and **(aq)** for aqueous (dissolved in water) are used to provide more information about the reaction conditions.
